title: 03. Multiprocessing: Day 4 — Advanced Multiprocessing: Pools & Shared Memory
summary: When you call pool.map(fn, items), the pool doesn't ship one task at a time — it ships chunks of tasks to each worker to amortize IPC overhead.
objectives: Use multiprocessing.Pool for high-throughput parallel workloads.
Choose between map, starmap, apply_async, imap, and imap_unordered based on workload.
Use Value, Array, and Manager to share state across processes safely.
Configure callbacks and error handlers on async pool results.
Benchmark threads vs processes vs asyncio on real workloads and interpret the results.
Avoid the most common multiprocessing footguns: un-picklable args, fork-with-threads, leaked pools.

sections.title: Theory & Visual Explanation
sections.body:
### 1. `Pool` — Process Management Done For You

```
                  ┌────────────────────────────────────┐
                  │           Process Pool             │
   submit() ────▶ │  ┌────┐ ┌────┐ ┌────┐ ┌────┐       │
                  │  │ W1 │ │ W2 │ │ W3 │ │ W4 │       │  ← N persistent workers
                  │  └─┬──┘ └─┬──┘ └─┬──┘ └─┬──┘       │
                  └────│──────│──────│──────│──────────┘
                       │      │      │      │
                       ▼      ▼      ▼      ▼
                  task queue (internal) — tasks distributed
                  result queue (internal) — results collected

  Pool benefits vs manual Process:
   ✓ Workers reused — no spawn cost per task
   ✓ Internal task queue — load balancing
   ✓ Result ordering and async callbacks
   ✓ Clean `with` block shutdown
```

### 2. Which Pool Method Should I Use?

| Method | When | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `map(fn, iterable)` | You need results in input order; can hold all in memory | `list` |
| `imap(fn, iterable)` | Like `map` but lazy — results stream as ready | iterator (ordered) |
| `imap_unordered(fn, iterable)` | Fastest — results stream as ready, in any order | iterator (unordered) |
| `starmap(fn, [(a, b), ...])` | Each item is itself a tuple of args | `list` |
| `apply_async(fn, args)` | One-off call, non-blocking, with callback | `AsyncResult` |
| `apply(fn, args)` | One-off call, blocking | result |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Iterable of tasks] --> B{Pool method}
    B -->|map| C[All results in input order]
    B -->|imap| D[Stream results, input order]
    B -->|imap_unordered| E[Stream results, any order]
    B -->|apply_async| F[AsyncResult object]
    B -->|starmap| G[Results, multiple args per call]
```

### 3. Chunksize — Why It Matters

When you call `pool.map(fn, items)`, the pool doesn't ship one task at a time — it ships **chunks** of tasks to each worker to amortize IPC overhead.

```
items = [1, 2, 3, ..., 1000]
chunksize = 4, 4 workers

W1 gets [1, 2, 3, 4]              → run, return [r1..r4]
W2 gets [5, 6, 7, 8]              → run, return [r5..r8]
...
```

**Heuristic:** `chunksize = len(items) // (4 * n_workers)` is a reasonable default for short tasks. For tasks that take >100ms each, `chunksize=1` is fine.

### 4. Shared Memory: `Value`, `Array`, `Manager`

```
┌─────────────── Process A ──────────────┐
│  local GIL  │  local GIL  │  local GIL │
│             │             │            │
│  Value('i', 0) ←─── shared via mmap ──→  Value('i', 0)
│             │             │            │
└─────────────┴─────────────┴────────────┘
   ↑ shared with all processes via mmap

Manager (separate server process):
   ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
   │   Manager server process             │
   │   holds dict / list / Value / ...    │
   └──────────────────────────────────────┘
       ↑            ↑            ↑
       │ proxy      │ proxy      │ proxy
   Process A    Process B    Process C
   (every access = IPC roundtrip = SLOW)
```

| Primitive | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| `Value(typecode, initial)` | Direct mmap — fast | Single scalar; manual locking |
| `Array(typecode, initial)` | Direct mmap — fast for arrays | Fixed size; manual locking |
| `Manager().Value()` | Works for any picklable type | Every read/write is IPC |
| `Manager().dict()` / `.list()` | Mutable shared containers | Very slow — use sparingly |

### 5. Threads vs Processes vs asyncio — Decision Tree

```
                       What does your workload look like?
                                    │
              ┌─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┐
              │                     │                     │
        Pure CPU work         Pure I/O work         Mixed (CPU + I/O)
              │                     │                     │
     multiprocessing           asyncio              Two options:
        (Pool) ✓              (asyncio) ✓           A) asyncio + run_in_executor(ProcessPool)
                                                    B) multiprocessing + threads in each worker
```

sections.title: Example 1 — Pool.map Parallel Image Processing
sections.body:
```python
"""Example 1: Parallel image processing with Pool.map."""
from __future__ import annotations

import logging
import multiprocessing as mp
import os
import time
from pathlib import Path

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def process_image(path: str) -> tuple[str, int]:
    """Simulate CPU-heavy image processing — return (path, bytes_processed)."""
    # In real code: open with PIL, apply filter, save.
    size = os.path.getsize(path) if os.path.exists(path) else 1024
    # Simulate CPU work proportional to size.
    total = 0
    for i in range(size * 10):
        total ^= i
    return path, total

def make_dummy_files(tmpdir: Path, n: int = 8) -> list[str]:
    tmpdir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    paths = []
    for i in range(n):
        p = tmpdir / f"img_{i:03d}.bin"
        p.write_bytes(b"\0" * (1024 + i * 100))
        paths.append(str(p))
    return paths

def main() -> None:
    tmpdir = Path("/tmp/pool_demo")
    paths = make_dummy_files(tmpdir, n=12)

    # Sequential baseline.
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    seq = [process_image(p) for p in paths]
    seq_time = time.perf_counter() - t0
    logger.info("sequential: %.2fs", seq_time)

    # Parallel.
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    with mp.Pool(processes=min(4, mp.cpu_count())) as pool:
        par = pool.map(process_image, paths)
    par_time = time.perf_counter() - t0
    logger.info("parallel:   %.2fs  (speedup: %.2fx)",
                par_time, seq_time / par_time)
    logger.info("results match: %s", seq == par)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

**Key points:** `map` returns results in the **same order** as the input, regardless of which worker finished first. The `with` block handles pool shutdown and worker cleanup.

sections.title: Example 2 — Pool.starmap for Multi-Argument Tasks
sections.body:
```python
"""Example 2: Pool.starmap — each task has multiple arguments."""
from __future__ import annotations

import logging
import multiprocessing as mp

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def compute(a: int, b: int, op: str) -> int:
    if op == "+":
        return a + b
    if op == "*":
        return a * b
    if op == "**":
        return a ** b
    raise ValueError(f"unknown op: {op}")

def main() -> None:
    tasks: list[tuple[int, int, str]] = [
        (2, 3, "+"),
        (4, 5, "*"),
        (2, 10, "**"),
        (100, 1, "+"),
        (7, 8, "*"),
    ]
    with mp.Pool(processes=4) as pool:
        results = pool.starmap(compute, tasks)

    for (a, b, op), result in zip(tasks, results):
        logger.info("%d %s %d = %d", a, op, b, result)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

**When to use `starmap`:** when each task needs multiple arguments. `map` only supports single-argument functions (you'd otherwise have to wrap args in a tuple and unpack inside `fn`).

sections.title: Example 3 — apply_async with Callback and Error Handler
sections.body:
```python
"""Example 3: Non-blocking submit with success and error callbacks."""
from __future__ import annotations

import logging
import multiprocessing as mp
import random
import time

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def risky_task(task_id: int) -> int:
    """Succeed 70% of the time; raise otherwise."""
    time.sleep(random.uniform(0.1, 0.5))
    if random.random() < 0.3:
        raise RuntimeError(f"task {task_id} failed deliberately")
    return task_id * 100

def on_success(result: int) -> None:
    logger.info("✓ success callback: result=%d", result)

def on_error(exc: BaseException) -> None:
    logger.error("✗ error callback: %s", exc)

def main() -> None:
    with mp.Pool(processes=4) as pool:
        # apply_async returns immediately; callbacks run in the MAIN process.
        async_results = [
            pool.apply_async(risky_task, (i,),
                             callback=on_success,
                             error_callback=on_error)
            for i in range(10)
        ]
        # Optional: wait for all with a global timeout.
        for ar in async_results:
            try:
                ar.get(timeout=5)  # re-raises if task failed and no error_callback
            except RuntimeError:
                pass  # already handled by error_callback
    logger.info("pool closed")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

**Important:** callbacks (`callback` and `error_callback`) execute in the **main process**, not in workers. They must be fast and side-effectful (logging, accumulating results). If they raise, the exception is silently swallowed — keep them simple.

sections.title: Example 4 — imap_unordered for Streaming Results
sections.body:
```python
"""Example 4: Process results as they finish, not in input order."""
from __future__ import annotations

import logging
import multiprocessing as mp
import random
import time

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def slow_task(task_id: int) -> int:
    """Variable duration — finishes in random order."""
    duration = random.uniform(0.1, 1.5)
    time.sleep(duration)
    return task_id

def main() -> None:
    n_tasks = 12
    t0 = time.perf_counter()

    with mp.Pool(processes=4) as pool:
        # imap_unordered yields results as they complete.
        for result in pool.imap_unordered(slow_task, range(n_tasks), chunksize=1):
            elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0
            logger.info("task %d done at +%.2fs", result, elapsed)

    logger.info("total: %.2fs", time.perf_counter() - t0)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

**Why `imap_unordered` rocks:** if task 5 finishes before task 0, you can start processing task 5's result immediately. Critical when downstream work depends on results being available ASAP (e.g., user-facing progress).

sections.title: Example 5 — Shared Value and Array with Manual Locking
sections.body:
```python
"""Example 5: Shared memory via Value and Array, with explicit locking."""
from __future__ import annotations

import logging
import multiprocessing as mp
import time
from multiprocessing.sharedctypes import Synchronized, SynchronizedArray

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def increment_value(counter: Synchronized, n: int) -> None:
    """Each worker adds n to the shared counter."""
    for _ in range(n):
        # `with counter.get_lock():` ensures atomic read-modify-write.
        with counter.get_lock():
            counter.value += 1

def fill_array(arr: SynchronizedArray, worker_id: int, start: int,
               end: int) -> None:
    """Each worker fills its slice of the shared array."""
    with arr.get_lock():
        for i in range(start, end):
            arr[i] = worker_id * 1000 + i

def main() -> None:
    # 'i' = signed int, 'd' = double, 'f' = float, 'b' = signed char
    counter = mp.Value("i", 0)  # type: Synchronized
    arr = mp.Array("i", 10)     # type: SynchronizedArray

    n_workers = 4
    increments_per_worker = 25_000
    procs = [
        mp.Process(target=increment_value, args=(counter, increments_per_worker))
        for _ in range(n_workers)
    ]
    for p in procs:
        p.start()
    for p in procs:
        p.join()

    logger.info("counter = %d (expected %d)",
                counter.value, n_workers * increments_per_worker)

    # Array example — 4 workers each fill 2-3 slots.
    chunk = 10 // n_workers or 1
    procs = [
        mp.Process(target=fill_array,
                   args=(arr, i, i * chunk, (i + 1) * chunk if i < n_workers - 1 else 10))
        for i in range(n_workers)
    ]
    for p in procs:
        p.start()
    for p in procs:
        p.join()
    logger.info("array contents: %s", list(arr))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

**Critical:** `counter.value += 1` is **not atomic** even though `counter` is shared — it's still a read-modify-write across multiple bytecodes. The `with counter.get_lock():` block is what makes it safe.

sections.title: Example 6 — Manager for Shared Dict and List
sections.body:
```python
"""Example 6: Manager provides shared dict / list / Namespace across processes."""
from __future__ import annotations

import logging
import multiprocessing as mp
import time

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def worker(worker_id: int, shared_dict: dict, shared_list: list) -> None:
    for i in range(3):
        shared_dict[f"key-{worker_id}-{i}"] = worker_id * 10 + i
        shared_list.append(f"W{worker_id}-{i}")
        time.sleep(0.05)

def main() -> None:
    with mp.Manager() as manager:
        shared_dict = manager.dict()
        shared_list = manager.list()

        procs = [mp.Process(target=worker, args=(i, shared_dict, shared_list))
                 for i in range(3)]
        for p in procs:
            p.start()
        for p in procs:
            p.join()

        logger.info("dict: %s", dict(shared_dict))
        logger.info("list: %s", list(shared_list))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

**Performance warning:** every `shared_dict[k] = v` is an IPC roundtrip to the Manager server process. For tight loops this is 100–1000× slower than a `Value`/`Array` or a local dict. Use `Manager` only when you genuinely need shared mutable containers.

sections.title: Example 7 — Benchmark: Threads vs Processes vs asyncio
sections.body:
```python
"""Example 7: Side-by-side benchmark for CPU-bound and I/O-bound workloads."""
from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
import multiprocessing as mp
import threading
import time
import urllib.request
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

# ───── CPU-bound task ─────

def cpu_task(n: int) -> int:
    """Sum of primes up to n."""
    return sum(1 for x in range(2, n)
               if all(x % p for p in range(2, int(x ** 0.5) + 1)))

def bench_cpu_sequential(n: int, chunks: int) -> float:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(chunks):
        cpu_task(n)
    return time.perf_counter() - t0

def bench_cpu_threads(n: int, chunks: int, n_workers: int) -> float:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(n_workers) as pool:
        list(pool.map(cpu_task, [n] * chunks))
    return time.perf_counter() - t0

def bench_cpu_processes(n: int, chunks: int, n_workers: int) -> float:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    with mp.Pool(n_workers) as pool:
        pool.map(cpu_task, [n] * chunks)
    return time.perf_counter() - t0

# ───── I/O-bound task ─────

URL = "https://httpbin.org/delay/1"

def io_task() -> int:
    with urllib.request.urlopen(URL, timeout=15) as resp:
        return len(resp.read())

def bench_io_sequential(n: int) -> float:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(n):
        io_task()
    return time.perf_counter() - t0

def bench_io_threads(n: int, n_workers: int) -> float:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(n_workers) as pool:
        list(pool.map(lambda _: io_task(), range(n)))
    return time.perf_counter() - t0

async def _async_io_task(session) -> int:
    import aiohttp
    async with session.get(URL) as resp:
        return len(await resp.read())

async def _bench_io_async(n: int) -> float:
    import aiohttp
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        await asyncio.gather(*[_async_io_task(session) for _ in range(n)])
    return time.perf_counter() - t0

def bench_io_async(n: int) -> float:
    return asyncio.run(_bench_io_async(n))

def main() -> None:
    print("=== CPU-bound (sum primes up to 50000, 4 chunks) ===")
    n_cpu = 50_000
    chunks = 4
    print(f"  sequential:  {bench_cpu_sequential(n_cpu, chunks):.2f}s")
    print(f"  4 threads:   {bench_cpu_threads(n_cpu, chunks, 4):.2f}s  (GIL-bound)")
    print(f"  4 processes: {bench_cpu_processes(n_cpu, chunks, 4):.2f}s  (true parallel)")

    print("\n=== I/O-bound (4 HTTP requests with 1s delay each) ===")
    n_io = 4
    print(f"  sequential:  {bench_io_sequential(n_io):.2f}s")
    print(f"  4 threads:   {bench_io_threads(n_io, 4):.2f}s")
    print(f"  4 asyncio:   {bench_io_async(n_io):.2f}s")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

**Expected output (rough):**

```
=== CPU-bound (sum primes up to 50000, 4 chunks) ===
  sequential:  3.20s
  4 threads:   3.45s  (GIL-bound)              ← no speedup
  4 processes: 0.95s  (true parallel)           ← ~3.4× speedup

=== I/O-bound (4 HTTP requests with 1s delay each) ===
  sequential:  4.10s
  4 threads:   1.15s
  4 asyncio:   1.05s
```

The benchmark validates the decision tree from the top of this guide.

sections.title: Day 4 Cheat Sheet
sections.body:
| Pattern | Snippet |
|---|---|
| Pool map | `with mp.Pool(4) as p: r = p.map(fn, items)` |
| Pool starmap | `p.starmap(fn, [(a, b), ...])` |
| Pool apply_async | `ar = p.apply_async(fn, args, callback=cb, error_callback=ecb)` |
| Stream unordered | `for r in p.imap_unordered(fn, items, chunksize=1):` |
| Shared scalar | `v = mp.Value("i", 0); with v.get_lock(): v.value += 1` |
| Shared array | `arr = mp.Array("i", 100)` |
| Shared dict | `with mp.Manager() as m: d = m.dict()` |
| CPU count | `mp.cpu_count()` |
| Pickle check | `pickle.dumps(obj)` in try/except |

**That wraps up threading + multiprocessing (Days 1–4). Next up: 6 days of async/asyncio deep dive, starting with the event loop and coroutines.**
